newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's landless take fight to pages of magazine.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's landless take fight to pages of magazine.

text.p: Brazil's Landless Movement, known for its high-profile tactic of invading vacant farms to press their demands for land reform, has taken its struggle to the pages of a quarterly magazine.

"We are more than just a group of people who carry out land invasions and protests, which is what you see in the press," Alipio Freire, editor of Landless Magazine, said late on Thursday at a ceremony marking the publication's launch.
"We want to show the other side of us," Freire said.
The first issue, to hit newsstands in two weeks, is 32 pages and features a black-and-white cover photograph of a bearded man clutching two daughters in his arms.

The photo, and several others in the first issue, were taken by Sebastiao Salgado, Brazil's internationally acclaimed photographer best known for capturing the developing world's squalor and misery in gripping black and white images.

The Landless Movement, which already has two Internet sites, is highly critical of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's effort to reform the economy through privatisations of state industry and slashing the public workforce.
It says the government has turned a blind eye to the four million landless Brazilian families. The government puts the figure at about one million families.

More than 100 people have been killed in land disputes in Brazil since Cardoso took office in January 1995. A police massacre of 19 peasants in April 1996 prompted Cardoso to declare land reform a priority but critics say he has not made good on promises to put more families on unused land.
About 50 percent of Brazil's arable land belongs to 2 percent of landowners.
